summary.title: Operating Systems: From 0 to 1
summary.one_liner: A self-study book that teaches you to write an operating system from scratch by reading hardware manuals, covering x86 assembly, ELF, linking, and debugging on bare metal with QEMU and gdb.
keywords: write an operating system from scratch
takeaways: How to write an OS from scratch by reading hardware datasheets and Intel manuals rather than relying on quick online answers
How x86 assembly, ELF, linking and loading, and debugging on bare metal fit together across hardware and software layers
Hands-on debugging of code running directly on hardware using gdb and QEMU
Status: Parts 1 and 2 (8 chapters) are complete; Part 3 is a set of implementation specifications, with its chapters still incomplete
A sample OS repository implements protected mode, TSS-based processes, interrupts and LAPIC; paging and I/O are not yet implemented
summary.summary: The book is a self-learning guide to building an operating system from zero, organized in three parts. Parts 1 and 2 (eight chapters) cover x86 assembly, the Intel manuals, ELF, linking, and debugging on bare metal with pure C and no standard library. Part 3 is a set of specifications for implementing OS components, with few code examples, and is described as a university-assignment style exercise. It lists prerequisites (basic electronics, C, Linux command line, touch typing) and a sample OS repository that implements protected mode, TSS processes, interrupts and LAPIC.
